statement: In adults with alcohol dependence in double-blind outpatient trials, most of them European and most after detoxification, acamprosate compared with placebo is associated with fewer people returning to any drinking during treatment: across 16 trials pooled in a review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 1,968 of 2,576 people on acamprosate (76 in 100) and 1,893 of 2,271 on placebo (83 in 100) drank again (crude totals, editors' arithmetic), a pooled difference of 9 in 100 (risk difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.04; 12 people treated for one to benefit), with large differences between trials (I² 80.8%) (Jonas et al., 2014; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared); its 2023 update gives a risk ratio of 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93; 20 trials, 6,380 people) and a Cochrane review 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91; 24 trials) (McPheeters et al., 2023; Rösner et al., 2010). In the Cochrane review abstinent days rose by about 11 in every 100 days (10.94 percentage points, 5.08 to 16.81; I² 94%), and in 7 trials fewer people on acamprosate had returned to drinking 3 to 12 months after treatment ended (risk ratio 0.91, 0.87 to 0.96). Acamprosate did not reduce return to heavy drinking (risk ratio 0.99, 0.94 to 1.05; 7 trials). In the 4 trials at low risk of bias the difference was not clear (risk difference −0.02, −0.09 to 0.05); the two of them with by far the most events, both in the US and one of them COMBINE, found no benefit, while most of the other 15 trials were European and recruited from inpatient settings or treatment programmes. The 2014 authors list population differences, other heterogeneity, chance or 'no true association between acamprosate and return to drinking' as possible explanations. Of the Cochrane review's 24 trials, 17 were run or supported by drug companies, mostly the manufacturer, though industry-run and non-profit trials gave similar estimates (risk ratios 0.88 and 0.88). Diarrhoea was more common (11 more in 100; risk difference 0.11, 0.09 to 0.13), and more people stopped because of side effects (risk ratio 1.35, 1.01 to 1.80). Head to head, acamprosate and naltrexone did not differ (return to any drinking risk ratio 1.03, 0.96 to 1.10; 3 trials). The three reviews share most of their trials. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
plain: In trials, mostly in Europe, fewer people with alcohol dependence who took acamprosate drank again during treatment than people on dummy pills: about 76 in 100 against 83 in 100. It did not cut heavy drinking. The most carefully run trials, including the two largest of them, both in the US, found no clear difference, and most trials were run or supported by companies that make it. Diarrhoea was more common: about 11 more people in every 100. Acamprosate and naltrexone did about the same when compared directly.
population: Adults with alcohol dependence in double-blind outpatient trials of 8 weeks to one year, mostly after detoxification and with psychosocial treatment in both groups; most placebo-controlled trials in Europe (16 of 22 in Jonas et al.; 19 of 24 in the Cochrane review)
exposure: Acamprosate tablets as given in the trials
comparator: Placebo with the same co-intervention; naltrexone in head-to-head trials
outcome: Return to any drinking during treatment and 3 to 12 months after it; abstinent days; return to heavy drinking; side effects and stopping because of them
magnitude: Jonas et al. 2014 (against placebo, trials at low or medium risk of bias): return to any drinking RD −0.09 (95% CI −0.14 to −0.04), 16 trials, 4847, I² 80.8%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; crude totals 1968/2576 (76.4%) against 1893/2271 (83.4%) (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2); by risk of bias, post hoc: high or unclear −0.13 (−0.20 to −0.06), 3 trials, 757; medium −0.11 (−0.16 to −0.06), 12 trials, 3438; low −0.02 (−0.09 to 0.05), 4 trials, 1409; return to heavy drinking −0.01 (−0.04 to 0.03), 7 trials, 2496; percentage of drinking days WMD −8.8 (−12.8 to −4.8), 13 trials; deaths 7 against 6 (8 trials, 2677), insufficient. McPheeters et al. 2023: return to any drinking RR 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93), 20 trials, 6380, moderate (I² 77.6%); return to heavy drinking 0.99 (0.94 to 1.05), 7 trials, moderate (no effect); percentage of drinking days −8.3 (−12.2 to −4.4), 14 trials; diarrhoea RR 1.58 (1.27 to 1.97). Rösner et al. 2010 (Cochrane): return to any drinking RR 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91), 24 trials, 6172, NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); abstinent days MD 10.94 percentage points (5.08 to 16.81), 19 trials, I² 94%; after treatment RR 0.91 (0.87 to 0.96), 7 trials, 1986; return to heavy drinking 0.99 (0.94 to 1.04), 6 trials, 2132; diarrhoea RD 0.11 (0.09 to 0.13), 16 trials; drop-out because of adverse events RR 1.35 (1.01 to 1.80), 19 trials; by funding, fully industry-sponsored 0.88 (0.80 to 0.97), 11 trials, partly industry-supported 0.84 (0.78 to 0.89), 6 trials, non-profit 0.88 (0.81 to 0.96), 7 trials. COMBINE: acamprosate main effect on percent days abstinent 78.4 against 77.6 (P=.61); time to first heavy drinking day HR 0.85 (0.63 to 1.15), the paper's main-effect hazard ratio, whose basis is unclear (study card sc_anton_2006).

evidence.extracted: Most placebo-controlled acamprosate trials were conducted in Europe (16 of 22) and a minority in the US (4 of 22); the few US-based acamprosate studies did not find it efficacious. European trials typically recruited from inpatient settings or treatment programmes and US trials through advertisements and referrals, which the authors suggest may have produced populations differing in severity and potential for benefit.

evidence.extracted: COMBINE, during treatment: no main effect of acamprosate on percent days abstinent (least-squares means 78.4 against 77.6 with placebo, P=.61; effect size 0.02, 97.5% CI −0.11 to 0.15) or on time to the first heavy drinking day (hazard ratio 0.85, 0.63 to 1.15), and no significant interaction involving acamprosate. The paper does not say how its main-effect hazard ratios were coded; by their intervals they may compare single groups rather than the whole factorial (a reporting issue on the study card).

risk_of_bias.note: Most trials were at medium risk of bias and the low-risk trials show no clear effect; allocation concealment was adequate in 3 of the Cochrane review's 24 trials; 17 of 24 trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly the manufacturer, and several outcomes came from manufacturer reports (study card sc_rosner_2010b). Industry and non-profit trials gave similar estimates, so funding is not rated separately.

inconsistency.note: Large unexplained heterogeneity for the main outcome (I² 80.8% in 2014, 77.6% in 2023; 94% for abstinent days) and a split between mostly European trials that found benefit and the largest US trials that did not; the explanations offered (recruitment, severity) were not tested.

indirectness.note: Worded for the trial populations (detoxified adults with alcohol dependence, mostly in Europe).

imprecision.note: The pooled intervals exclude no effect; the low-risk subgroup is imprecise, which is part of the inconsistency rating and not counted twice.

publication_bias.note: Not detected (funnel plots and Begg's or Egger's tests in two reviews); the 2023 review did not assess it.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias and for inconsistency, giving low, below the reviews' moderate grades, because the effect is not seen in the trials at low risk of bias and the 2014 authors name bias as one possible explanation. Worded as an association, as the 2014 review words it, because the randomized design would support causal wording but the evidence leaves open whether the pooled effect is real. Overlap: the three reviews share most trials, and COMBINE and Mason 2006 are in all of them, so they are counted once. Status mixed: trials point both to a modest benefit (mostly European) and to none (the largest low-risk US trials), with no adequate explanation; the critique comes from inside the review itself, and the claim does not take a side beyond the low certainty.
